# Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array.

@example The smallest value is 12 and the largest 45. Both are multiples of 3, and of no larger number.
[18,45,12,30]
=> 3

@example 64 is a multiple of 16, so the answer is 16 itself. The 25 in between has no divisor above 1 in common with 16, but it doesn't take part.
[40,25,16,64]
=> 16

@example 9 and 14 have no common divisor above 1.
[14,9,11]
=> 1

# The smallest possible value: 1 divides everything.
[1,1000]
=> 1

# All values equal, at the top and at the bottom of the range: a minimum
# that starts at a constant such as 999, or a maximum that starts at 2,
# goes wrong here.
[1000,1000]
=> 1000

[1,1,1]
=> 1

# The greatest common divisor of the whole array would be 5; only 10 and
# 20 count.
[10,15,20]
=> 10

# The extremes sit in the middle, the largest before the smallest: the
# first and last values, 50 and 60, would give 10. 999 = 27 * 37.
[50,999,333,37,60]
=> 37

# 998 and 1000 share 2; the first and last values, 999 and 998, share 1.
[999,1000,998]
=> 2

# The largest value comes first and every later value is a new smallest.
# A scan that tests "smaller?" and only otherwise "larger?", with the
# largest starting below every value, never records 84 and returns 56.
[84,70,56]
=> 28

# The largest value is a multiple of the smallest.
[7,700,350]
=> 7

# Repeated extremes; the 35 between them would bring the answer down to 5.
[20,50,20,35,50]
=> 10

# A common divisor that is neither value: 640 = 2 * 320, 960 = 3 * 320.
[640,960,800]
=> 320

[24,18]

[27,9,9,9,18,27]
=> 9

=> 1

[22,22]
=> 22

[703,374,657,496,375,704,407]
=> 22

@gen 7 small
[26,11]
=> 1
